39-198.r: Species that form symbiosis occur in cnidarians (corals with dinoflagellate algae), fungi and protozoa → all three.

39-199.r: Mycorrhiza → symbiosis of fungi with roots of higher plants; plant gains phosphorus and nitrogen absorption and protection from root diseases.
39-199.c: The book answers (a) Protection, but its own explanation gives both better mineral absorption and disease protection, which is option (d).

39-202.r: Lichens → symbiotic association of algae and fungi; can start ecological succession even on bare rock.

39-204.r: Alga–fungus partnership in lichen → mutualism: alga (chlorophyll partner) makes food; fungus protects it.

39-206.r: Lichens → do not grow in polluted areas; sensitive to SO2, as they absorb nutrients straight from the air without filtering.

39-207.r: Lichens → good bioindicators of air pollution (SO2) (1 correct); they do not grow well in polluted areas (2 wrong).

39-208.r: Root-nodule bacteria of legumes (e.g. Rhizobium) → symbiotic; they convert nitrogen gas (N2) into ammonium compounds.

40-001.r: Cell → structural and functional unit of life.

40-002.r: Besides the nucleus, DNA is found in mitochondria (and chloroplasts).

40-003.r: Viroids → short circular single-stranded RNA without a protein coat (smallest pathogens, mostly of plants); prions are infectious proteins, not cells; Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall.

40-004.r: Plant cells: cellulose cell wall and one large vacuole; animal cells: no wall, many small vacuoles. Both have a plasma membrane (statement 2 wrong).

40-005.r: Plant cell differs from animal cell mainly by its cellulose cell wall (also green plastids).

40-007.r: Mitochondria (0.5-1.0 µ diameter) → 'powerhouse' of the cell; the nucleus stores DNA and coordinates cell activities.
hi: Powerhouse of the cell (कोशिका का ऊर्जाघर)

40-010.r: Plasma (cell) membrane → two layers of phospholipids with embedded proteins, i.e. lipid + protein.

40-011.r: Biological membranes → lipid bilayer and proteins in combinations specific to each species, cell type and organelle (fluid mosaic model).

40-012.r: Protein synthesis → ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER is studded with ribosomes).

40-013.r: Apoptosis → programmed cell death; removes old, unnecessary and unhealthy cells.

40-014.r: Most ATP → last (terminal) respiratory series, i.e. oxidative phosphorylation: about 27-34 of the 30-38 ATP made per glucose.

41-001.r: Father of (modern) genetics → Gregor Johann Mendel, discoverer of the laws of inheritance.

41-004.r: Mendel's experiments → garden pea, seven traits; three laws: Dominance, Segregation, Independent Assortment.

41-005.r: Mendel's principle of inheritance → based on sexual reproduction.

41-006.r: Genome mapping → mapping of genes: locating genes and the distances between them on a chromosome.

41-007.r: Gene → basic physical and functional unit of heredity, made of DNA (in humans from a few hundred to over 2 million bases).

41-008.r: Gene → a segment of DNA (generally 5000-100000 nucleotide pairs).

41-009.r: Genetic code → universal; triplet codons for 20 amino acids; non-overlapping, non-ambiguous, commaless; has start and stop codons (64 codons) → all true.

41-010.r: Nonsense (stop) codons → UAA, UAG, UGA; AUG, UUU and UGC are sense codons.
41-010.h: UAA 'U Are Away', UAG 'U Are Gone', UGA 'U Go Away'.

41-011.r: Mutation → change in the base sequence of a gene; heritable, the ultimate source of genetic variation.

41-012.r: Not true: 'nucleus has no role in cell reproduction' – it holds and copies DNA for daughter cells. True: chromosomes = DNA + protein; genes = functional DNA segments.

41-013.r: Hereditary traits pass to offspring through chromosomes (nucleoproteins carrying genes); term 'chromosome' coined by Waldeyer.

41-014.r: DNA → controls hereditary characters; some viruses (Tobacco Mosaic Virus, QB bacteriophage) use RNA instead.

41-015.r: DNA can store and pass on genetic information because its two strands are complementary (A pairs with T, G with C).

41-016.r: Sexual reproduction → variation through blending of genes, chromosomal changes and shuffling of genes (all of the above).

41-017.r: Chromosomal theory of inheritance → Walter Sutton (1902, 1903) and Theodor Boveri; chromosomes carry the genetic material.

41-018.r: DNA double-helix structure → James Watson and Francis Crick (1953); Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins got the 1962 Nobel Prize.

41-023.r: Double-helix model → Watson and Crick (1953); DNA itself was first isolated by Friedrich Miescher (1869).
41-023.t: Discovery of DNA (Miescher, 1869) ≠ its double-helix structure (Watson-Crick, 1953).

41-025.r: Har Gobind Khorana → 1968 Nobel (with Holley, Nirenberg) for interpreting the genetic code and its role in protein synthesis; also made DNA in the laboratory.

41-027.r: 'Jumping genes' → Barbara McClintock, from heredity studies in corn; Nobel Prize 1983.

41-028.r: Tyrosine (4-hydroxyphenylalanine) → one of the 22 amino acids, not a DNA compound; adenine, guanine, cytosine are DNA bases.

41-029.r: Sugar in DNA → deoxyribose, a variant of the five-carbon sugar ribose.

41-030.r: Ribozymes → RNA enzymes (catalytic RNA), e.g. in ribosomes; Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman, Nobel 1989.

41-031.r: Chromosome number → constant for a species; does not change with age or weight.

41-032.r: Lizards → no morphologically recognisable sex chromosomes (shown in genus Sceloporus).

41-033.r: Humans → 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 pairs autosomes + 1 pair sex chromosomes (female XX, male XY).

41-035.r: A false: child's sex depends on whether the male gives X or Y. R true: women have two X chromosomes. Y (male) + X (female) → boy.
41-035.h: Mother always gives X; father decides.

41-038.r: Highest risk of permanent DNA change → X-ray technician (not carbon-14 researchers, coal miners or dyers).

42-001.r: Biofertilizers → cultures of living or dormant beneficial microbes (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum); organic and green manures are not biofertilizers.

42-002.r: Azolla and blue-green algae → used as biofertilizers (microbes that raise nutrient uptake in the rhizosphere); alfalfa is not.

42-004.r: Rhizobium, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) and Azolla → all biofertilizers that help fix nitrogen.

42-005.r: Not nitrogen-fixing → mycorrhiza (fungus–plant association); Nostoc, Anabaena and Azotobacter fix nitrogen.

42-006.r: Azolla → nitrogen-fixing biofertilizer, widely used in Southeast Asia; not yeast, Chlorella or mould.

42-008.r: Azolla → biofertilizer also used as supplementary feed for cattle, especially milch animals.

42-009.r: Wrong pair: Azotobacter – bioinsecticide; Azotobacter is a bacterium fixing nitrogen in the rhizosphere. Correct: blue-green algae–biofertilizer, Chrysopa–Maho control, Bio 902–mustard.

42-010.r: Biological nitrogen fixation → blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), not red, brown or green algae.

42-011.r: Blue-green algae → biofertilizer chiefly for paddy (rice); supplies nitrogen.

42-013.r: Wrong pair: Azolla – Maize (Azolla serves paddy). Correct: blue-green algae–paddy, Rhizobium leguminosarum–pea, Azotobacter–wheat.

42-014.r: Azolla (an aquatic fern) → good biofertilizer with blue-green algae (cyanobacteria); supplies nitrogen to rice fields.

42-019.r: Azolla (floating aquatic fern; Azolla pinnata is rich in nitrogen) → biofertilizer of water-logged rice fields; not Wolffia, Trapa or Lemna.

42-020.r: Phosphatic biofertilizer → VAM (Arbuscular Mycorrhiza fungi), aiding phosphorus uptake; Rhizobium, blue-green algae and Azolla fix nitrogen.

42-021.r: Biochar (charcoal from pyrolysis of organic waste) → used in vertical-farming growing media, promotes nitrogen-fixing microbes, helps retain water → all three correct.

42-022.r: Wrong statement: 'earthworms slow composting'; earthworms and microbes speed up decomposition of farm waste in compost pits.

42-023.r: Nitrogen use efficiency rises with split application, nitrogen inhibitors and slow-release nitrogen fertilizers → all of the above.

42-024.r: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in root nodules of legumes (pulse crops).

42-025.r: Nitrogen-fixing (legumes, Fabaceae, with Rhizobia in root nodules) → alfalfa, chickpea, clover; not amaranth, purslane (kulfa) or spinach.

42-026.r: Paddy → does not fix nitrogen; legumes (gram, pea, bean) do, via Rhizobium in root nodules turning air nitrogen into ammonia.

42-027.r: Nitrogen fixation in soybean → Rhizobium japonicum.

42-028.r: Leghaemoglobin → in legume root nodules (alfalfa, soybean); supplies oxygen to nodule bacteria for nitrogen fixation.

42-029.r: Earthworms → 'ploughers of the soil': aerate soil, let in air and water, break down organic matter.

43-001.r: Body weight is mostly water: generally 55-70% (adult about 65%); infants 75-78%, dropping to 65-70% by one year.

43-004.r: Most abundant element in the human body → oxygen (mainly as water); six elements (O, C, H, N, Ca, P) make about 99% of body mass.

43-005.r: Of iron, sodium, phosphorus, calcium → calcium is most abundant. Body: O 65%, C 18.5%, H 9.5%, N 3.2%, Ca 1.5%, P 1.0%.

43-006.r: Main salt in bones → calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite, about 70% of bone by weight); highest element in body → oxygen.

43-008.r: Adult human body → 206 bones (about 300 at birth; some fuse together).

43-011.r: Smallest bone → stapes (stirrup-shaped, in the middle ear); largest bone → femur (thigh).

43-013.r: Human skull (excluding hyoid) → 28 bones: cranium 8 + face 14 + middle-ear bones 6.

43-014.r: Cervical (neck) vertebrae → 7 (C1 atlas, C2 axis … C7).

43-015.r: Atlas–axis (atlantoaxial) joint → synovial pivot joint between the first two neck vertebrae; turns the head side to side.

43-016.r: Joint where neck joins head → pivot (pivotal) joint, a synovial joint allowing head rotation.

43-017.r: Ribs → 12 pairs (total 24); with the sternum they form the rib cage protecting heart and lungs.

43-018.r: Leg (long) bone → hollow: its shaft (diaphysis) is a hollow cylinder of compact bone holding fat-storing yellow marrow.

43-019.r: Osteoclasts → bone cells that break down bone tissue for remodelling and repair; the book accepts (a) bone formation and (c) bone fracture.

43-020.r: Arthroplasty → joint replacement surgery, e.g. hip-joint replacement with a synthetic implant.

43-021.r: Cartilage → firm but flexible tissue, softer than bone, can bend (outer ear, nose tip); carpals are the eight wrist bones.

43-022.r: Ligament → dense fibrous connective tissue joining two bones at a joint.

43-023.r: Dental plaque → bacterial biofilm of food particles, saliva, mouth acids and bacteria; saliva pH 6.2-7.6 (average 6.7).

43-024.r: No pain on cutting nails → nails are dead layers of α-keratin with no nerves or blood vessels.

43-025.r: Alpha-keratin → fibrous protein of the skin's outer layer (epidermis); also in hair, nails and hooves.

43-026.r: Hair → protein keratin, also the main part of finger and toe nails.

43-027.r: Hair and nails → keratin, a strong protein also in skin, hooves, horns and teeth.

43-028.r: Bones and teeth → need calcium and phosphorus (plus other minerals).

43-029.r: Bones and teeth need calcium, phosphorus and fluorine; iodine is not needed for them (it is used by the thyroid gland).

43-030.r: 20 teeth develop twice (milk and permanent sets; diphyodont); the 12 permanent molars come only once (monophyodont).

43-031.r: Strongest part of the body → tooth enamel (hydroxyapatite, mainly calcium phosphate); its destruction causes tooth decay.

43-032.r: Wrong: 'muscles can only push bones'. Muscles work in pairs and become shorter, stiffer and thicker when they contract.

43-033.r: Smallest muscle → stapedius, in the middle ear; it steadies the stapes bone and controls its vibration.

43-034.r: Strongest muscle (by weight) → masseter, the jaw muscle; jaw muscles close the teeth with up to about 90.7 kg force on molars.

43-035.r: Breastbone → Sternum; Collarbone → Clavicle; Knee-cap → Patella; Shoulder blade → Scapula.

44-001.r: Most digestion → small intestine (over 20 feet long), using pancreatic enzymes and bile from the liver.

44-002.r: Tongue tastes → sweet, bitter, salty, umami, sour; 'spicy' (a pain signal) and 'pungent' (linked to smell) are not tastes.

44-003.r: Bitterness → the back (posterior part) of the tongue is most sensitive; all parts can sense all tastes.

44-004.r: Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth (buccal cavity): salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose and dextrin.

44-005.r: Saliva (about 99.5% water) → helps digest starch through amylase; also has lysozyme and IgA.

44-007.r: Amylase (in saliva) → hydrolysis of starch; not invertase, dehydrogenase or anhydrase.

44-008.r: A true: liver aids fat digestion through bile, which emulsifies fats. R false: liver makes no fat-digesting enzymes; bile has no enzymes.

44-009.r: Hydrochloric acid → secreted in the stomach by parietal (oxyntic) cells; kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen.

44-011.r: Enzymes → biocatalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living systems.

44-016.r: Enzymes → biocatalysts (1 correct) and generally act at the site where they are produced (2 correct) → both.

44-017.r: Zymase (enzyme complex in yeast) → ferments sugar (glucose) into ethanol and CO2.

44-018.r: Liver → converts harmful ammonia into urea; also makes bile and stores fat. It is the largest gland.

44-019.r: Lipid digestion → lipase (fats → fatty acids + monoglycerides) and bile acids (emulsify fats); pepsin digests proteins, not fats.

44-020.r: Lipase (fat-digesting enzyme) → produced in the pancreas (also mouth and stomach).

44-021.r: Gastrin → a hormone that stimulates stomach acid (HCl), not a digestive enzyme; trypsin (pancreas), ptyalin (saliva), pepsin (stomach) are enzymes.

44-022.r: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, by pepsin from the gastric glands.

44-023.r: Stomach protein enzyme → pepsin only (pepsinogen activated by HCl); trypsin and chymotrypsin come from the pancreas and act in the small intestine.

44-024.r: Pepsin → proteins into peptides and amino acids; lactase: lactose → glucose + galactose; urease: urea → CO2 + ammonia; zymase: yeast fermentation.

44-025.r: A false: protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin), not only in the small intestine. R true: pancreatic trypsin is released into the small intestine.

44-027.r: Trypsin (in the duodenum) → hydrolyses peptide bonds, breaking proteins into smaller peptides; other proteases then turn them into amino acids.
44-027.c: The book answers (c) proteins to amino acids, but its own explanation says trypsin breaks proteins into smaller peptides, which is option (b).

44-028.r: Appendix → blind tube attached to the caecum, the start of the large intestine.

44-029.r: Small intestine parts by decreasing length → ileum > jejunum > duodenum (duodenum is C-shaped, about 20-25 cm).

44-030.r: A true: humans cannot digest cellulose (no enzyme for it). R true: salivary diastase breaks starch into maltose, but R does not explain A.

44-031.r: Correct pair: E. coli restriction endonuclease (EcoRII) → cuts DNA at specific sites; used to make recombinant DNA.

44-032.r: Ptyalin → digests starch; Pepsin → digests proteins; Renin → angiotensinogen to angiotensin; Oxytocin → contracts smooth muscle (uterus).

44-033.r: Vitamin → Carotene; Enzyme → Pepsin; Hormone → Testosterone/Progesterone; Protein → Keratin.

44-034.r: Carbohydrates are finally broken down to glucose (monosaccharides) for absorption; glucose is the cells' main energy source.

44-035.r: Extra glucose → converted to glycogen and stored in the liver.

44-036.r: Energy stored in liver and muscles → glycogen, the storage form of glucose.

44-037.r: Fasting over 10 days → glucose level in the liver falls, as stored glycogen is used up to supply glucose.

44-038.r: Gallstones (cholesterol, bilirubin) block bile reaching the duodenum → mainly affect fat digestion.

44-039.r: Largest gland → liver (about 22 cm long, 15 cm wide, about 1.5 kg); also the largest internal organ.

44-041.r: Bile → made by the liver; stored and concentrated in the gallbladder.

44-043.r: Bile from liver and gallbladder → enters the small intestine at the duodenum (its first part).

44-044.r: Pancreas → second-largest gland; its alkaline pancreatic juice is called a 'complete digestive juice'; liver is the largest gland.

44-045.r: Secretin → from the duodenum in response to HCl (acidity); enterogastrone → from the small intestine in response to fatty acids → both correct.

45-001.r: Growth and repair of tissues → proteins; cheese (also pulses, soybean, milk, eggs) is a protein source.

45-002.r: Probiotic food → contains live beneficial bacteria and helps maintain gut flora → both correct.

45-003.r: Probiotics → live bacteria and yeasts (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces boulardii); they occur naturally in our gut (2 wrong) and help digest milk sugars.

45-004.r: Nutraceuticals → foods or supplements giving nutrients plus a medicinal (health) benefit.

45-005.r: Casimir Funk → coined 'vitamins' ('vital amines'); earlier, Umetaro Suzuki (1910) extracted 'aberic acid' from rice bran.

45-006.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin D – Paul Muller. McCollum (spelt 'Maculan') → vitamins A, B, D; James Lind → vitamin C (citrus cures scurvy).

45-007.r: Vitamins → organic compounds needed in small amounts; the body cannot make enough, so they come from the diet.

45-008.r: 'Accessory food factor' (idea of F. G. Hopkins) → vitamins.
